name: Turn Meter
description:
Who acts next, by speed. Every combatant has a meter that fills at its own pace, and whoever fills first takes the turn. The meter is DISCRETE: between turns every meter is advanced by exactly the time the soonest one needs, so a unit twice as fast acts twice as often, and the order is a function of the stats — replayable from the same roster, with no die in it. Asked for after the turn meter in RAID-style squad battlers, and written as a component for any turn-based pack rather than as one game's screen.

IT REPLACES INITIATIVE, NOT THE QUEUE. combat.turn_order_queue still announces whose turn it is, counts the rounds, takes input.endTurn and input.delayTurn and ends an exhausted turn; where this component is in the build the queue asks it for the order instead of rolling a die, re-asked after every turn, and a round is as many turns as there are combatants. A second component that announced turns of its own would be the two-answers problem the queue exists to end, so this one never says whose turn it is — only who is full and who is next.

ACTING EMPTIES THE METER. Delaying keeps `delayKeeps` of it, which is what makes delay a bet rather than a skip: a unit that yields comes back sooner than one that acted. A unit that joins the fight late (combat.aggroGained) starts empty, and a dead one leaves the meter the way it leaves the board — the roster owns who is alive, so this asks rather than deciding.

It publishes `meters`, each combatant's fill as a fraction, which is the readout players plan against in every game with a meter, and `order`, the next `previewLength` turns as the simulation says they fall. The prediction is honest because the simulation IS the rule: there is no other order for it to differ from. Status effects are not read yet; a slowed unit fills at its stat until something owns slowing as a number rather than as a count.

implementations.note: Implemented in the consuming application; not verifiable from this repository.

inputs.name: fillAt
inputs.description: The meter is full at this, and a unit's speed is what it gains per unit of time. The scale is cosmetic — a stat of 10 against 100 fills in ten units of time, and time here is only a count — but every meter players have ever read goes to 100, so 100.

inputs.name: speedStat
inputs.description: Which roster stat is speed. Dexterity is the tactics default and the queue's tie-break; movement makes the far-walking units the often-acting ones, which some games want. A stat of zero is read as one, so nobody is seated who can never act.

inputs.name: previewLength
inputs.description: How many turns ahead `order` predicts. The rail along the top of a battle screen shows about this many; the simulation is cheap, but a prediction nobody can see is a cost without a reader.

inputs.name: delayKeeps
inputs.description: The fraction of a full meter a unit keeps when it delays rather than acts. Zero makes delay cost a whole turn, which makes it a skip; one would let a unit sit at the front of the line forever, so it is clamped below that.

outputs.name: meters
outputs.description: Each combatant in the fight: `id`, `fill` as a fraction of full (0..1), and `speed`. Fullest first. Exactly one is full at the start of a turn — the one whose turn it is.

outputs.name: order
outputs.description: Unit ids, the next `previewLength` turns in the order the meter says they fall, the full one first. The queue reads this as its order; the rail draws it.

outputs.name: speedOf
outputs.description: A unit's speed as this component counts it, for a readout that wants to say why one unit acts more often than another.

provenance: Asked for after RAID-style squad battlers, where the turn meter is the fight's whole tempo. Nothing in the catalogue ordered turns by a stat over time (searched 2026-10-27: combat.turn_order_queue rolls initiative once a round and fixes it; combat.energy_per_turn and combat.action_point_economy budget a turn, not its timing; combat.super_meter fills from blows and spends on a move). Library-native, written to feed the queue's order rather than to announce turns of its own.
